    "pathomechanism": "The six-month history of chest pain and fatigue indicates primary Lung Qi deficiency compounded by post-surgical trauma. Post-surgical trauma consumes Qi and blood reserves, leaving the body in a depleted state that can persist for 3-6 months or longer. The recurrence of nodules in the contralateral lung suggests a constitutional tendency toward pathogenic qi stagnation and possible chronic inflammatory state—in TCM, prolonged Qi obstruction in the thoracic region can lead to blood stasis and mass formation.   "analysis": {
    "summary": "This 57-year-old female presents with a half-year history of chest pain and fatigue following surgical treatment of lung nodules, now with recurrence in the contralateral lung. The half-year timeline places her in the post-surgical recovery phase, during which Qi and blood depletion from surgical trauma typically persist; fatigue at this stage is expected but suggests incomplete reserve restoration.\n\nThe recurrence of nodules in the opposite lung is particularly concerning from both biomedical and TCM perspectives. Biomedically, it raises the possibility of aggressive disease, metastasis, or a systemic predisposition (infection, genetic predisposition, or environmental exposure). From a TCM standpoint, it suggests a constitutional weakness—likely deficient Qi and defensive function—that has allowed pathogenic factors (heat, damp-heat, chronic inflammation, or blood stasis) to take root despite surgical intervention. The preserved appetite, sleep, and mood are encouraging signs indicating the Spleen has not collapsed and retains recovery potential.\n\nWithout pulse examination (which would clarify whether this is simple deficiency or deficiency with stagnation), tongue diagnosis (to assess Spleen, Lung, and Kidney reserve), or detailed palpation of the chest (to localize qi obstruction), this assessment must be considered preliminary. The recommendations that follow are appropriate for post-surgical Lung Qi deficiency but should be refined after a complete in-person TCM evaluation. Most critically, recurrent pulmonary nodules demand urgent biomedical imaging and oncologic re-evaluation—TCM supportive care cannot replace this necessity, and any delay in medical surveillance could have serious consequences.",

      "from_visual": "No tongue, face, or body observations provided in the data submitted. This severely limits diagnostic confidence.       "from_pulse": "No pulse data provided. Critical missing information. Expected findings for this pattern: weak, thin pulse (Qi deficiency); possible thin-rapid if heat component present; possible choppy quality if blood stasis component present; quality and location (cun/guan/chi positions) would help differentiate Lung vs. Spleen vs. Kidney involvement and assess treatment urgency",
      "from_other": "Post-surgical status is the dominant context—all findings must be interpreted as recovery-phase, not primary disease onset. The recurrence is the critical clinical flag requiring immediate biomedical workup before TCM treatment proceeds."

    "pattern_rationale": "Lung Qi deficiency is identified as primary based on: (1) Chief symptom of fatigue directly corresponds to Lung Qi deficiency (Lung controls Qi and houses Po, the corporeal soul); (2) Chest pain/discomfort is classic Lung qi stagnation or Lung Qi deficiency presentation; (3) Post-surgical trauma always damages Qi reserves, and six months post-op with persistent fatigue indicates inadequate recovery; (4) The Lung is the organ most directly affected by pulmonary nodules and surgery; (5) Fatigue without severe appetite loss points to Spleen involvement (source of post-heavenly Qi) rather than constitutional collapse. Heart-Lung involvement is secondary because chest pain can reflect both Lung qi circulation and Heart blood circulation; the Heart houses consciousness and emotional stability, and the preserved mood at presentation argues against primary Heart Shen disturbance, but Heart-Lung communication should still be supported due to chest localization. Spleen Qi weakness is confirmed because the Spleen is the primary organ for Qi production from food—weak Spleen explains fatigue despite good appetite. Blood stasis as secondary component is suggested by nodule formation (stagnation creates masses) and recurrence (incomplete resolution), but without purple tongue or dark complexion, full blood stasis pattern is less likely than Qi stagnation with mild blood involvement. The post-surgical qi and blood depletion framework is classical TCM recovery medicine and applies to all surgical patients; this patient's persistence of symptoms suggests either inadequate supplementation or complicating factors (disease recurrence, inflammation) not fully apparent from the data provided."

  "disclaimer": "This Traditional Chinese Medicine assessment is provided for informational and complementary care purposes only and must NOT be considered a substitute for professional biomedical medical diagnosis, treatment planning, surveillance, or ongoing medical care. The patient must continue all scheduled medical imaging, laboratory testing, specialist consultations, and monitoring appointments regardless of TCM treatment. This assessment does not create a doctor-patient relationship and does not obligate the patient to follow any recommendations; all medical decisions remain the patient's choice in consultation with their licensed healthcare providers."

diagnosis.primary_pattern: Lung Qi Deficiency with Heart-Lung Qi Insufficiency
secondary_patterns: Possible localized qi stagnation with mild blood stasis in thoracic region (evidenced by recurrent nodule formation)
diagnosis.pathomechanism: The six-month history of chest pain and fatigue indicates primary Lung Qi deficiency compounded by post-surgical trauma. In TCM theory, the Lung controls respiration, houses Qi, and opens to the chest—deficiency of Lung Qi manifests as fatigue and chest discomfort. The Spleen is the secondary organ involved, as it is responsible for generating post-heavenly Qi from food; the fatigue pattern suggests Spleen Qi weakness insufficient to support recovery. Post-surgical trauma consumes Qi and blood reserves, leaving the body in a depleted state that can persist for 3-6 months or longer. The recurrence of nodules in the contralateral lung suggests a constitutional tendency toward pathogenic qi stagnation and possible chronic inflammatory state—in TCM, prolonged Qi obstruction in the thoracic region can lead to blood stasis and mass formation. However, the preservation of appetite, sleep, and mood at initial presentation is a favorable prognostic sign, indicating the Spleen retains sufficient function to serve as an anchor for recovery.
diagnosis.disease_cause: Primary cause: Post-surgical Qi and blood depletion following nodule resection. Secondary cause: Constitutional Lung Qi deficiency predisposing to recurrent pulmonary pathology and impaired healing. Tertiary factor: Possible inadequate recovery of Defensive Qi (Wei Qi), the body's immune barrier, leaving the patient vulnerable to recurrent disease and tissue changes.

constitution.characteristics: Fatigue as primary presentation despite preserved appetite and sleep suggests underlying insufficiency in Qi production and mobilization rather than severe systemic collapse. The constitution is characterized by low energy reserves, difficulty with post-operative recovery, and probable tendency toward chronic respiratory vulnerability.
constitution.tendencies: Prone to slow wound healing, recurrent or persistent respiratory conditions, fatigue after minimal exertion, tendency toward mass formation (as evidenced by repeated nodule development), increased infection risk due to compromised Defensive Qi, general difficulty recovering from trauma or surgery
constitution.percentage_match: Strong pattern match estimated at 70-80%, with confidence limited by absence of pulse data, tongue examination, and facial observation. Full Four Examinations in person would refine this assessment.

analysis.summary:
This 57-year-old female presents with a half-year history of chest pain and fatigue following surgical treatment of lung nodules, now with recurrence in the contralateral lung. Based on the limited clinical data provided, the pattern most consistent with her presentation is Lung Qi deficiency as the primary dysfunction, with secondary involvement of the Spleen (as source of post-heavenly Qi) and Heart (due to chest localization and possible qi-blood imbalance). The half-year timeline places her in the post-surgical recovery phase, during which Qi and blood depletion from surgical trauma typically persist; fatigue at this stage is expected but suggests incomplete reserve restoration.

The recurrence of nodules in the opposite lung is particularly concerning from both biomedical and TCM perspectives. Biomedically, it raises the possibility of aggressive disease, metastasis, or a systemic predisposition (infection, genetic predisposition, or environmental exposure). From a TCM standpoint, it suggests a constitutional weakness—likely deficient Qi and defensive function—that has allowed pathogenic factors (heat, damp-heat, chronic inflammation, or blood stasis) to take root despite surgical intervention. The preserved appetite, sleep, and mood are encouraging signs indicating the Spleen has not collapsed and retains recovery potential.

Without pulse examination (which would clarify whether this is simple deficiency or deficiency with stagnation), tongue diagnosis (to assess Spleen, Lung, and Kidney reserve), or detailed palpation of the chest (to localize qi obstruction), this assessment must be considered preliminary. The recommendations that follow are appropriate for post-surgical Lung Qi deficiency but should be refined after a complete in-person TCM evaluation. Most critically, recurrent pulmonary nodules demand urgent biomedical imaging and oncologic re-evaluation—TCM supportive care cannot replace this necessity, and any delay in medical surveillance could have serious consequences.

key_findings.from_inquiry: Six-month symptom duration indicates chronic post-surgical recovery pattern, not acute inflammation; chest pain localized to thorax suggests Lung qi obstruction or Heart-Lung disharmony; fatigue without complete appetite loss or insomnia indicates Spleen Qi weakness rather than Spleen Yang collapse; preserved mood and sleep are favorable recovery indicators; recurrent nodules on opposite side suggest systemic vulnerability rather than simple scar-related dysfunction and raise urgent need for biomedical assessment of disease progression
key_findings.from_visual: No tongue, face, or body observations provided in the data submitted. This severely limits diagnostic confidence. Ideally a full in-person examination is required to assess: tongue color (pale = Qi deficiency, dark red = heat/stasis), coat thickness (thick = stagnation), facial complexion (pale = Qi/blood deficiency), body habitus (weight loss = disease progression vs. normal post-op), and extremity warmth (cold = Qi-Yang deficiency)
key_findings.from_pulse: No pulse data provided. Critical missing information. Expected findings for this pattern: weak, thin pulse (Qi deficiency); possible thin-rapid if heat component present; possible choppy quality if blood stasis component present; quality and location (cun/guan/chi positions) would help differentiate Lung vs. Spleen vs. Kidney involvement and assess treatment urgency
key_findings.from_other: Post-surgical status is the dominant context—all findings must be interpreted as recovery-phase, not primary disease onset. The recurrence is the critical clinical flag requiring immediate biomedical workup before TCM treatment proceeds.

analysis.pattern_rationale: Lung Qi deficiency is identified as primary based on: (1) Chief symptom of fatigue directly corresponds to Lung Qi deficiency (Lung controls Qi and houses Po, the corporeal soul); (2) Chest pain/discomfort is classic Lung qi stagnation or Lung Qi deficiency presentation; (3) Post-surgical trauma always damages Qi reserves, and six months post-op with persistent fatigue indicates inadequate recovery; (4) The Lung is the organ most directly affected by pulmonary nodules and surgery; (5) Fatigue without severe appetite loss points to Spleen involvement (source of post-heavenly Qi) rather than constitutional collapse. Heart-Lung involvement is secondary because chest pain can reflect both Lung qi circulation and Heart blood circulation; the Heart houses consciousness and emotional stability, and the preserved mood at presentation argues against primary Heart Shen disturbance, but Heart-Lung communication should still be supported due to chest localization. Spleen Qi weakness is confirmed because the Spleen is the primary organ for Qi production from food—weak Spleen explains fatigue despite good appetite. Blood stasis as secondary component is suggested by nodule formation (stagnation creates masses) and recurrence (incomplete resolution), but without purple tongue or dark complexion, full blood stasis pattern is less likely than Qi stagnation with mild blood involvement. The post-surgical qi and blood depletion framework is classical TCM recovery medicine and applies to all surgical patients; this patient's persistence of symptoms suggests either inadequate supplementation or complicating factors (disease recurrence, inflammation) not fully apparent from the data provided.

treatment.therapeutic_principle: Tonify Lung Qi and Spleen Qi as the foundation for recovery; gently move Qi stagnation in the chest to resolve pain and prevent mass formation; support Heart-Lung communication to normalize blood and Qi circulation; strengthen Defensive Qi to reduce recurrence risk
treatment.treatment_method: Primary: Herbal tonification with qi-building and Lung-supporting formulas (Liu Jun Zi Tang and/or Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang). Secondary: Acupuncture and acupressure to Lung Source point (LU9), Qi Sea point (CV6), chest qi-moving points (REN17), and Lung transporting point (UB13), combined with systemic tonification points (ST36). Tertiary: Dietary therapy with warming, qi-building foods and avoidance of qi-depleting foods; lifestyle modification emphasizing rest and gentle movement; emotional regulation to prevent worry-related Qi stagnation.

beneficial: Chicken or bone broth (especially with Astragalus/Huang Qi root, 15g per liter)—Warm, sweet flavor directly tonifies Lung and Spleen Qi; post-surgical patients require protein and amino acids for tissue repair, and broth is easily absorbed without straining Spleen digestion
Millet (小米, xiao mi) or glutinous rice (糯米, nuo mi)—Sweet, neutral temperature; enters Spleen and tonifies Spleen Qi more gently than white rice; easier to digest for a Spleen-weak constitution

Goji berries (Gou Qi Zi, 枸杞子, 10-15g daily)—Sweet, neutral; tonifies Lung Yin and Qi simultaneously; supports Kidney reserve and may help prevent recurrent disease; commonly used in post-surgical recovery formulas

Tremella (White Fungus, Bai Mu Er, 白木耳, 15-30g)—Sweet, neutral; moistens Lung, tonifies Lung Qi, and has mild immune-supporting properties; specifically used in classical TCM recovery tonics post-surgery

Shiitake mushrooms (Lentinula edodes, 香菇) or Reishi mushrooms (Ganoderma, 灵芝)—Warm to neutral; support Qi circulation and immune function; gentle adaptogenic effect without overstimulation; shiitake is commonly available and well-tolerated
recipes: Astragalus and Chicken Qi Tonic Broth (黃芪雞湯): Ingredients: 1 whole chicken (1.5 kg) or 600g chicken breast, 20g Astragalus root (Huang Qi, 黃芪), 10g Ginseng (Ren Shen, 人參), 8 Chinese red jujubes (Hong Zao, 紅棗), 3 slices fresh ginger (Sheng Jiang, 生薑), 2 liters water. Method: Blanch chicken briefly to remove scum, rinse. Combine all ingredients in a pot, bring to boil, then reduce to low simmer for 90 minutes until chicken is very tender. Strain broth, discard solids or shred chicken to return to broth. Consume 1 cup (250 ml) twice daily (morning and evening), 5 days per week for 4-6 weeks. This is the classic post-surgical Qi tonification formula in food form; the warm Qi-tonifying herbs combined with protein-rich broth directly addresses post-operative depletion.

Tremella and Goji Qi-Tonifying Porridge (白木耳枸杞粥): Ingredients: 30g Tremella (Bai Mu Er, soaked in hot water 20 minutes), 15g Goji berries (Gou Qi Zi), 100g glutinous rice (Nuo Mi, 糯米, not regular white rice), 1 liter water, optional 1 tsp honey (add after cooking). Method: Bring water to boil, add soaked Tremella (torn into small pieces) and rice, simmer on low for 45-60 minutes until creamy and rice is very soft. Add Goji berries in the last 5 minutes. Divide into 2 portions. Consume one portion warm in the morning on an empty stomach or light pre-breakfast, and one portion in the evening 1-2 hours before bed. Daily for 5-6 days per week for 6-8 weeks. This porridge tonifies Lung Qi and Yin while being exceptionally easy to digest for a post-surgical Spleen—the tremella and glutinous rice are both bland and warming, ideal for recovery.

foods_to_avoid: Greasy, deep-fried foods (fried chicken, French fries, fried snacks, fatty meats)—create damp-heat and obstruct Qi circulation in the chest; worsens qi stagnation and chest pain; inhibits Spleen Qi tonification

Pungent and stimulating foods in excess (raw garlic, raw onion, excess chili peppers, black pepper, ginger in large quantities)—scatter Qi upward and can trigger or worsen chest discomfort and palpitations post-surgery; can destabilize recovering Qi during vulnerable recovery phase

Cold and raw foods (ice cream, iced beverages, frozen fruits, raw salads, cucumber, watermelon, raw fish)—severely damage Spleen Yang and Cold accumulates in the digestive system, reducing Spleen's Qi-transforming ability and prolonging fatigue; especially contraindicated in post-surgical Spleen-weak patients
lifestyle: Avoid strenuous exercise and heavy lifting for at least 3 months post-surgery—Qi consumed during intense exertion before reserves are rebuilt; instead, practice slow walking at comfortable pace (20-30 minutes daily) or gentle Tai Chi/Qigong to mobilize Qi without depleting reserves; this is a medical safety principle, not just TCM advice

Maintain consistent sleep schedule with 22:00-06:00 as primary window, with special attention to sleeping during 03:00-05:00 (Lung's peak activity time in TCM)—Poor sleep directly worsens Lung Qi dysfunction and delays recovery; consistent sleep enables the body's natural repair mechanisms and supports Lung qi restoration

Practice gentle breathing exercises or meditation for 10-15 minutes daily (Eight Pieces of Brocade, Tai Chi breathing, or simple diaphragmatic breathing—in for 4 counts, hold for 4, out for 6)—Stress and worry directly damage Lung Qi; these practices mobilize Qi, reduce chest tension, calm the Shen (spirit), and prevent qi stagnation from emotional causes

Keep chest and torso warm, avoid direct air conditioning or fan exposure on the body—Wind-Cold invades weakened post-surgical Lung Qi and can trigger recurrence or complications; dress in layers, use a blanket when resting, and avoid cold environments; this is particularly important given the pulmonary vulnerability
acupoints: LU9 Taiyuan (太淵, Greater Abyss)—Located on the palm side of the wrist at the wrist crease (proximal wrist fold), on the lateral (thumb) side in the depression between the radial artery and the tendon of flexor carpi radialis; you will feel the radial pulse here. Massage firmly with the thumb pad in small circular motions for 2-3 minutes, 1-2 times daily (morning and evening preferred). This is the Source (Yuan) point of the Lung channel and the most important single point for Lung Qi tonification; directly addresses fatigue and Lung dysfunction.

ST36 Zusanli (足三里, Leg Three Miles)—Located on the lower leg 3 cun directly below the kneecap (below ST35 Dubi, which is on the lateral side of the patellar ligament below the patella), positioned one finger-breadth (thumb-width) lateral to the anterior tibial crest (the bony ridge of the shin). Firm thumb pressure in small circles for 3-5 minutes, 1-2 times daily. This is the most important point in all TCM for Qi tonification and Spleen support; essential for post-surgical recovery and fatigue.

CV6 Qihai (氣海, Sea of Qi)—Located on the anterior midline of the abdomen 1.5 cun below the umbilicus (halfway between the navel and the pubic bone). Gentle circular massage with the palm or palm heel for 2-3 minutes, 1-2 times daily (morning and evening). Tonifies Qi throughout the entire body; addresses the root cause of fatigue.

REN17 Danzhong (膻中, Chest Center) or CV17—Located on the anterior midline of the chest at the 4th intercostal space (the horizontal line connecting the two nipples, directly between them, at the level of the heart). Gentle circular massage with the palm (NOT deep pressure on the ribs) for 2-3 minutes, 1-2 times daily. Moves Qi stagnation in the chest region and normalizes Heart-Lung communication; essential for chest pain resolution.

UB13 Feishu (肺俞, Lung Transporting Point)—Located on the back of the body at the level of the 3rd thoracic vertebra (T3, approximately at the level of the lower edges of the shoulder blades), 1.5 cun lateral to the midline of the spine. Ask a partner to massage in gentle downward strokes for 2-3 minutes, 1-2 times daily, or use a back massage tool or gua sha scraper in gentle downward strokes along the back parallel to the spine. This point directly impacts Lung physiology and is especially beneficial for post-surgical Lung recovery.

EX-HN3 Yintang (印堂, Hall of Seal) / Third Eye Point—Located on the forehead at the midpoint between the inner ends of the two eyebrows. Gentle pressure with the thumb pad for 1-2 minutes, 1-2 times daily. While not a classical Lung point, it calms the Shen and reduces anxiety/worry that drives Qi stagnation; useful for sleep support and emotional regulation in recovery.
exercise: Eight Pieces of Brocade (Ba Duan Jin, 八段錦) or Tai Chi Qigong—20-30 minutes per session, 5-6 days per week. These are traditional gentle flowing movement sequences that harmonize Qi circulation, strengthen Lung and Spleen function, and rebuild Qi reserves without depleting them. Practice at a leisurely pace focusing on deep diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing with each movement. Ideal for post-surgical recovery and fatigue.

Walking meditation (散步, San Bu) combined with breathing practice—30 minutes daily at a comfortable pace (able to speak full sentences without breathlessness). Walk slowly and mindfully, coordinating breathing with footsteps (inhale for 4 steps, exhale for 6 steps). This gently mobilizes Qi and Blood circulation without fatigue, supports Lung Qi, and aids emotional regulation.
recommendations.emotional_care: Post-surgical patients with recurrent disease commonly experience anxiety, fear, and depressive thoughts. In TCM theory, Worry (Si, 思) directly damages Spleen Qi and Grief (You, 憂) damages Lung Qi—these emotional patterns can block recovery and even contribute to disease progression through Qi stagnation. Daily emotional practices are essential: (1) Journaling or gratitude practice for 5-10 minutes daily to shift mindset from fear of recurrence to acceptance and hope; (2) Use REN17 (Danzhong, chest center) as a meditation anchor—place the palm on the chest and breathe slowly for 5-10 minutes while mentally affirming healing and strength; (3) Weekly gentle acupuncture or Tuina massage if available to release chest tension and reduce anxiety somatically; (4) Avoid excessive focus on medical test results and recurrence monitoring—excessive vigilance creates chronic Qi stagnation that paradoxically worsens outcomes; instead schedule monitoring appointments and then redirect attention to recovery activities; (5) If anxiety is severe or persistent, ask the TCM practitioner about herbal formulas like Gui Pi Tang (Restore the Spleen Decoction) or Tian Wang Bu Xin Dan (Emperor of Heaven's Special Pill to Tonify the Heart) which specifically support emotional stability alongside qi tonification.

herbal_formulas.name: Liu Jun Zi Tang (Six Gentlemen Decoction)
ingredients: Ren Shen (人參, Panax ginseng root, 9g)
Bai Zhu (白術, Atractylodes macrocephala rhizome, 9g)
Fu Ling (茯苓, Poria cocos sclerotium, 9g)
Zhi Gan Cao (炙甘草, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root honey-fried, 6g)
Ban Xia (半夏, Pinellia ternata rhizome, 6g)
Chen Pi (陳皮, Citrus reticulata aged peel, 6g)
herbal_formulas.dosage: Traditional decoction: 1 packet (above quantities) decocted in 3 cups water reduced to 1 cup, divided into 2 doses taken morning and evening on an empty stomach (30 minutes before food), 5-6 days per week for 4-6 weeks, then reassess. Alternatively, as concentrated granules: 6-9 grams mixed with warm water, 2-3 times daily between meals. Duration should be minimally 4 weeks to assess effectiveness.
herbal_formulas.purpose: Primary tonification of Spleen Qi (the source of post-heavenly Qi responsible for fatigue) and transformation of any dampness-phlegm that may underlie the tendency toward mass formation. This is the foundational formula for Spleen-Stomach Qi deficiency. The sweet bland tonifying herbs (Ginseng, Licorice, Atractylodes) supplement Qi, while the transformative herbs (Pinellia, Poria, Tangerine Peel) prevent stagnation and damp accumulation that could feed nodule development. This formula is ideal for the patient with preserved appetite who simply needs stronger Qi production.

herbal_formulas.name: Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang (Tonify the Middle and Augment the Qi Decoction)
ingredients: Huang Qi (黃芪, Astragalus membranaceus root, 15g)
Ren Shen (人參, Panax ginseng root, 9g)
Bai Zhu (白術, Atractylodes macrocephala rhizome, 9g)
Zhi Gan Cao (炙甘草, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root honey-fried, 6g)
Dang Gui (當歸, Angelica sinensis root, 9g)
Sheng Ma (升麻, Cimicifuga dahurica rhizome, 6g)
Chai Hu (柴胡, Bupleurum chinense root, 6g)
Chen Pi (陳皮, Citrus reticulata aged peel, 4.5g)
herbal_formulas.dosage: Traditional decoction: 1 packet (above quantities) decocted in 3 cups water reduced to 1 cup, divided into 2 doses taken morning and evening on an empty stomach, 5-6 days per week for 6-8 weeks post-surgery. Alternatively, as concentrated granules: 6-9 grams mixed with warm water, 2-3 times daily between meals. This formula is more potent than Liu Jun Zi Tang and better suited to aggressive post-surgical depletion.
herbal_formulas.purpose: More potent Qi tonification specifically suited to immediate post-surgical recovery with persistent fatigue. Astragalus (Huang Qi) is renowned for supporting Defensive Qi (Wei Qi) recovery—the immune barrier weakened by surgery and responsible for preventing infection and recurrence. The addition of Dang Gui supports Blood tonification (often depleted alongside Qi in surgery), while the qi-moving herbs (Bupleurum, Sheng Ma, Tangerine Peel) prevent the stagnation that leads to mass formation and recurrence. This is the 'workhorse' formula for post-operative patients with serious recovery needs, particularly those at risk for complications like recurrent disease.

herbal_formulas.name: Yu Ping Feng San (Jade Windscreen Powder / Jade Screen Powder)
ingredients: Huang Qi (黃芪, Astragalus membranaceus root, 15g)
Bai Zhu (白術, Atractylodes macrocephala rhizome, 9g)
Fang Feng (防風, Saposhnikovia divaricata root, 9g)
herbal_formulas.dosage: Concentrated granules: 6-9 grams mixed with warm water, 2-3 times daily between meals. Alternatively, raw herbs decocted in 2 cups water reduced to 1 cup, divided into 2 doses daily. Best taken as an ongoing maintenance formula for 8-12 weeks or longer (3-6 months total) to rebuild and stabilize the defensive layer.
herbal_formulas.purpose: Specifically strengthens Lung Qi and Defensive Qi (Wei Qi, the body's immune/protective barrier). Post-surgical patients are severely immunocompromised, and recurrent disease indicates failure of this defensive layer. This three-herb formula is ideal for prevention of recurrence and long-term immune stabilization. Astragalus and Atractylodes tonify the deep Qi, while Saposhnikovia 'astricts' and stabilizes the defensive layer, preventing pathogenic factors from invading. This can be used as a long-term maintenance formula even after Liu Jun Zi Tang or Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang is completed, as it addresses the root immunological vulnerability.

warning_signs: New or rapidly worsening chest pain, especially if sudden, severe, pleuritic (sharp with breathing), or radiating to arm, jaw, or shoulder—seek immediate cardiac and pulmonary emergency evaluation to exclude myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, or pneumothorax

New or progressive shortness of breath, wheezing, stridor, or difficulty speaking—urgent pulmonary imaging (chest X-ray or CT) required to exclude pneumonia, pleural effusion, tumor progression, or recurrence
Hemoptysis (coughing up blood or blood-tinged sputum)—immediately warrants pulmonary evaluation and imaging; strong indicator of active pulmonary pathology

Fever >38.5°C lasting more than 3 days or accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain—suggests post-surgical infection, pneumonia, or systemic infection; requires immediate medical evaluation

Rapid or unexplained weight loss >2 kg per month, persistent loss of appetite, or early satiety—red flag for disease progression, malignancy, or serious systemic pathology; requires immediate oncologic re-evaluation and imaging

Neurologic changes including new confusion, severe headache, focal weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking—possible complications including intracranial disease or metastasis; requires immediate neuroimaging

Severe fatigue that worsens despite rest and treatment, or sudden acute exacerbation of fatigue—may indicate disease progression, anemia from bleeding, or systemic inflammation; requires laboratory and imaging assessment
contraindications: Do NOT use TCM as a substitute for ongoing biomedical surveillance imaging. Lung nodules are serious pathology and recurrence must be monitored through CT or PET imaging on a regular schedule determined by your oncologist, not through symptom observation alone.

Do NOT assume improvement in symptoms equals disease control. Symptoms may improve from TCM support while imaging shows disease progression—conversely, imaging may show stability while symptoms persist. Always verify the correlation between symptom improvement and imaging findings with your medical team.

Do NOT delay medical follow-up or oncologic consultation in hope that TCM will achieve cure. The recurrence of nodules in the contralateral lung is a serious sign requiring urgent biomedical re-staging, possible additional imaging (PET-CT, biomarkers), and possibly additional medical intervention (chemotherapy, targeted therapy, radiation, or surgery).

Do NOT attempt to use aggressive 'anti-cancer' herbal formulas (such as those marketed as tumor-fighting or cancer-curing) without explicit permission from your biomedical oncology team. Some herbs can interact with chemotherapy drugs, affect blood clotting post-surgery, or interfere with targeted therapies. Simple tonifying formulas like those listed above are safe; aggressive formulas should be vetted by both TCM and conventional providers.

Do NOT use warming or heating herbs (such as Fu Zi/Aconite, Rou Gui/Cinnamon in large doses, or other pungent-warm herbs) without guidance, especially if biomedical tests show signs of inflammation or fever. Heat-generating herbs may exacerbate inflammatory pathology if the nodules are inflammatory in nature.

Do NOT postpone scheduled medical imaging, lab work, or specialist appointments due to TCM treatment or recovery from acupuncture. Maintain the full biomedical surveillance schedule recommended by your oncology team alongside any TCM care.
precautions.special_notes: CRITICAL CLINICAL NOTE: This patient presents with SERIOUS BIOMEDICAL PATHOLOGY that is beyond the scope of standalone TCM treatment. Lung nodules with histology suggesting possible malignancy, chronic infection, or idiopathic pulmonary disease, combined with RECURRENCE in the contralateral lung, are RED FLAG findings requiring urgent medical re-evaluation. The recurrence pattern is particularly concerning and suggests either: (1) aggressive disease course; (2) inadequate initial treatment; (3) new primary lesion reflecting systemic vulnerability; (4) chronic inflammatory or infectious process not fully controlled. TCM recommendations provided here are STRICTLY COMPLEMENTARY to ongoing biomedical care and are intended to support post-operative recovery, reduce symptom burden (chest pain, fatigue), optimize immune function, and prevent further deterioration. Under NO circumstances should TCM delay or replace urgent biomedical imaging (CT chest ± contrast, PET-CT if available), oncologic re-evaluation, tumor marker assessment (if applicable), and possible additional medical or surgical intervention. DIAGNOSTIC DATA LIMITATION: This assessment is based on very limited diagnostic information. The absence of pulse examination, tongue diagnosis, detailed palpation, facial observation, and other components of the Four Examinations TCM diagnostic framework means this pattern assessment has moderate-to-low confidence. A complete in-person TCM evaluation by a licensed practitioner is ESSENTIAL before initiating herbal treatment, as the diagnosis may require refinement based on full examination findings. For example, if pulse examination reveals rapid heat-pattern pulse, heat-clearing herbs may be needed; if tongue is dark purple, blood-moving herbs may be required; if palpation reveals chest-wall tenderness, local points and gua sha may be more beneficial than systemic tonification. Additionally, the recurrent nodule formation itself is not a pattern that TCM can monitor or treat—only biomedical imaging can assess this. Therefore, recommend: (1) IMMEDIATE: Complete biomedical re-staging including imaging and oncologic consultation; (2) URGENT (within 1 week): In-person TCM evaluation by licensed practitioner; (3) PARALLEL: Continue biomedical surveillance on schedule while TCM supportive care is initiated; (4) FOLLOW-UP: Monthly biomedical imaging as recommended by medical team, with TCM follow-ups every 2-4 weeks to adjust support as recovery progresses.

follow_up.timeline: TCM reassessment in 2 weeks via telehealth if dietary and acupressure home-care are initiated immediately. URGENT: Complete in-person TCM Four Examinations examination within 1 week of this assessment—the limited diagnostic data here means treatment recommendations should be refined significantly after pulse, tongue, and palpation examination. CRITICAL: Biomedical imaging (CT chest ± contrast, baseline labs including CBC, metabolic panel, tumor markers if applicable) should be completed immediately if not done within the past 1 month—do not delay imaging for TCM evaluation. Biomedical follow-up imaging on the schedule determined by your oncology team (typically every 3 months initially for new diagnosis, then adjusting based on findings).
follow_up.expected_improvement: IF biomedical workup shows stable disease without progression: (1) Fatigue should decrease by 30-40% within 4 weeks of consistent herbal supplementation and dietary therapy; (2) Sleep quality and appetite may normalize within 1-2 weeks as Spleen function improves; (3) Chest pain should decrease by 50% or more within 6-8 weeks with combination of acupressure, acupuncture, and herbal treatment. (4) Overall sense of strength and recovery capacity should noticeably improve by 6-8 weeks. HOWEVER: IF biomedical imaging shows disease progression, new nodules, or expansion of existing nodules, aggressive medical intervention becomes the absolute priority and expectations for TCM improvement shift—the focus would shift to palliative support rather than recovery tonification. In that scenario, no symptomatic improvement should be expected from TCM alone without simultaneous medical treatment.
follow_up.next_steps: STEP 1 (URGENT, day 1): Schedule biomedical imaging (CT chest) and oncology consultation if not completed in past month—do not delay. STEP 2 (URGENT, within 1 week): Complete in-person TCM Four Examinations examination (pulse, tongue, palpation, full history) with a licensed TCM practitioner to refine this preliminary assessment. STEP 3 (Within 1-2 weeks): If biomedical workup shows stable disease, initiate one of the herbal formulas recommended above—Liu Jun Zi Tang for gentle support, or Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang for more aggressive post-surgical recovery support. Begin dietary modifications and daily acupressure at home immediately. STEP 4 (Ongoing): Seek weekly acupuncture by licensed acupuncturist if available—acupuncture is more effective than self-acupressure alone for chest pain relief and Qi mobilization. STEP 5 (Monthly): Maintain scheduled biomedical imaging per oncology team's recommendation; do NOT deviate from or extend intervals. STEP 6 (Every 2-4 weeks): TCM follow-up visits to assess progress, adjust herbal formulas based on response, and provide ongoing acupuncture/Tuina support. ESCALATION: If at any point biomedical imaging shows disease progression or recurrence worsens, immediately escalate to medical oncology, pause non-essential supplements pending MD approval, and shift TCM focus to symptom palliation rather than recovery tonification.

parsed.disclaimer: This Traditional Chinese Medicine assessment is provided for informational and complementary care purposes only and must NOT be considered a substitute for professional biomedical medical diagnosis, treatment planning, surveillance, or ongoing medical care. Lung nodules, especially with recurrence in the contralateral lung, are SERIOUS medical conditions that may indicate malignancy, chronic infection, inflammatory lung disease, or other significant pathology requiring urgent biomedical evaluation, imaging, oncologic consultation, and potentially aggressive medical or surgical intervention. TCM care is designed to complement, not replace, conventional medicine in this context. This assessment is based on limited diagnostic data (absence of complete Four Examinations examination including pulse, tongue, and detailed palpation), which significantly limits confidence in the pattern diagnosis and treatment recommendations. A complete in-person TCM evaluation with a licensed, regulated TCM practitioner is essential before treatment is initiated. The patient must continue all scheduled medical imaging, laboratory testing, specialist consultations, and monitoring appointments regardless of TCM treatment. If at any time symptoms worsen, new warning signs appear, or biomedical workup shows disease progression, seek immediate medical attention and inform all healthcare providers of any TCM herbs or supplements being taken, as interactions are possible. TCM practitioners and clinicians in different geographic regions are regulated differently; verify that any provider consulted is licensed and in good standing in your region. The herbal formulas recommended are traditional classical formulas with long safety records when prescribed appropriately, but all herbal medicines carry some risk of side effects or interactions, particularly in patients with serious underlying disease or taking multiple medications. Never self-prescribe herbal formulas of unknown origin or quality—source formulas from reputable pharmacies with quality assurance. This assessment does not create a doctor-patient relationship and does not obligate the patient to follow any recommendations; all medical decisions remain the patient's choice in consultation with their licensed healthcare providers.

data.wen_inquiry: Chief complaint: Half a year of chest pain and fatigue; lung nodules found and later a recurrence in the other lung after surgery. Symptoms: chest pain; fatigue; good appetite, sleep and mood noted at first visit.

expected.source_pattern: Qi and Blood deficiency (deficiency of vital energy and blood)
